text:
The scoreboard said ANA 5, WPG 1, but the game was far closer than that. Anaheim's expected goals were 3.76 to 2.34, and the simulated replays of every shot gave the Ducks the win only 53 percent of the time. Winnipeg had 53 shot attempts to 39 and matched Anaheim at 17 shots on goal each. Through two periods the chance quality was nearly level (1.66 to 1.40 for ANA), and a Judd Caulfield snap shot in the first and a Tim Washe snap shot in the second were all that separated the teams.

The third period is where it broke open. Anaheim generated 2.09 expected goals to Winnipeg's 0.94, and Sam Colangelo made it 3-0 at 4:25 on a 28 percent chance. Kyle Connor cut it to 3-1 at 10:36, but Mikael Granlund answered at 14:06 with a wrist shot that carried a 2 percent chance of going in, the least likely goal of the night. Nikita Nesterenko added an 83 percent look at 19:19 to close it out. Clay Stevenson allowed 4 goals on 16 shots, about 1.5 more than the chances against him deserved.

Lukas Dostal made 16 saves on 17 shots, 1.34 goals better than expected, and Winnipeg's 0 for 4 on the power play (0.60 expected goals) never gave it a way back in. Anaheim also blocked 20 shots to Winnipeg's 9 and took the puck away less often than it gave it up, yet the Jets had nine takeaways to the Ducks' two. Caulfield and Washe each finished with a goal and an assist, and Jeff Malott had two assists, but the margin owed as much to a 2 percent goal and a goalie gap as to anything Winnipeg failed to do.
